summary: Defines a framework and requirements for call control and multi-party use of SIP, with an abstract call model for the media relationships these features need. The model is independent of how signaling or mixing is done. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is a plan for how phones manage calls with many people, such as holding, transferring and conferences, however the details work.

questions: how do call transfers work in sip
subtitle: Framework for handling multi-party calls, transfers, and conferences in SIP.

tldr.problem: SIP was originally designed for point-to-point calls, but real phone systems need call holding, transferring, conferencing, and more. It is unclear how to build these features in an interoperable way.
tldr.mechanism: This framework defines a conversation space model (participants sharing media), distinguishes signaling approaches (centralized third-party control versus peer-to-peer), and catalogs basic call control primitives that can be combined to build complex features.
tldr.outcome: Implementers have a common foundation for designing multi-party features that work across different signaling and mixing architectures, reducing feature interactions and supporting both traditional and distributed call control models.

today: RFC 5850 is Informational and provides the foundational framework for SIP call control. It remains the basis for SIP conferencing and multi-party feature implementations, though specific protocols for individual features (like RFC 5589 for transfer) continue to evolve.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs a Call Control Framework
sections.content:
SIP was defined for initiating and terminating multimedia sessions, but it was originally focused on point-to-point calls between two parties. Real telephone systems need to handle held calls, call transfers, call waiting, call forwarding, and conferences with many participants.

The problem is that SIP itself does not define how to manipulate dialogs (call legs) to create these features. Without a clear framework, every vendor implements these features differently, and complex combinations of features (like a transfer of a conferenced call) become unpredictable.

This document establishes common ground: it defines the abstract model of what a multi-party call is, shows how different signaling and mixing approaches work, and lists the basic primitives from which features can be built.
sections.eli5: Old phones had operators and switches that handled all the complex stuff. SIP is just for point-to-point calls, so someone has to say how to make the fancy features like putting someone on hold or transferring them.

sections.title: The Conversation Space Model
sections.content:
At the heart of the framework is the conversation space: an abstract set of participants who believe they are communicating with each other. Each conversation space has one or more participants. A participant is a user agent (UA) that sends or receives media; intermediaries like mixers, transcoders, or relays are not participants.

Participants can be active (smart enough to leave when they are done) or passive (like someone on hold). Some participants may be hidden (a supervisor monitoring a call for training, a recording service, or a tone generator announcing arrivals).

A simple two-party call is one conversation space with one dialog. A three-way call where one user mixes locally is also one conversation space but involves two dialogs. A centralized conference might have one conversation space but many dialogs, one between each participant and the mixer.
sections.eli5: A conversation is all the people who think they are talking to each other. Some people are visible, some are hidden. Some are smart, some are dumb (waiting for instructions).

sections.title: Two Signaling Approaches
sections.content:
The framework identifies two main signaling models:

Centralized third-party call control (3pcc): A controller sends all SIP requests on behalf of the participants. It creates dialogs with basic operations (INVITE, reINVITE, BYE) and manipulates them to rearrange the media relationships. The advantage is simplicity: endpoints need only basic SIP support. The downside is that all state lives in the controller, and new features must be implemented there.

Peer-to-peer: Participants send SIP requests directly to each other to create, modify, or destroy their dialogs. This requires endpoints to understand additional extensions like Replaces (to replace one dialog with another) or Join (to combine two conversation spaces). The advantage is that endpoints can retain state and take advantage of end-to-end features. The disadvantage is more complexity in clients.

The framework is designed to work with both approaches, and implementations can mix them.
sections.eli5: One way: a central boss sends all the orders. Everyone listens and obeys. Another way: everyone talks to everyone else directly. The boss is just a participant like anyone else.

sections.title: How Media Gets Mixed
sections.content:
When multiple participants need to hear each other, their media must be combined. The framework describes several mixing models:

End system mixing: One participant (e.g., user A) talks to two others (B and C) separately and mixes the audio locally. A hears B and C, sends a mix of itself and C to B, and a mix of itself and B to C. This needs no infrastructure, just a UA that can handle multiple dialogs.

Centralized mixing: All participants have dialogs with a central mixer. The mixer receives from all participants and sends mixed output to each. This scales better but requires a mixer component.

Distributed media with centralized signaling: A central controller sets up signaling, but media flows directly between endpoints using multicast or multi-unicast. Each endpoint mixes its own media.
sections.eli5: One person can listen to two others and mix them locally. Or a central mixer gets everyone's audio and sends each person a mix of the others. Or everyone sends to everyone directly and mixes their own.

sections.title: Catalog of Call Control Primitives
sections.content:
The framework catalogs call control actions that operate on dialogs. These are the basic building blocks:

Actions on single dialogs: remote answer (tell a UA to accept a ringing call), remote forward (tell it to redirect), remote hangup (tell it to hang up), remote dial (tell it to initiate a call), and remote hold (put a call on hold).

Actions on multiple dialogs: transfer (replace yourself with someone else in a conversation), take (forcibly replace someone else with yourself), add (bring a new person into a conversation), local join (merge two separate conversations), insert (place yourself between two parties), and split (break a conference into multiple conversations).

Real features like call forwarding, call waiting, call pickup, and conferencing are built by combining these primitives. The framework is designed so that only the person invoking a feature needs to understand that feature; other participants just experience the resulting media relationships.
sections.eli5: The basic moves are: answer a ringing call, hang it up, put it on hold, transfer someone to someone else, add a third person, grab a call that is in progress, or split up a group call.

sections.title: Naming and Invoking Features with SIP URIs
sections.content:
SIP URIs are powerful: they can name users, services, and resources. The framework uses SIP URIs as the interface to call control. A URI can be a conference room, a queue, a music-on-hold service, an announcement server, or a media server component.

Features are invoked through URIs embedded in SIP requests (e.g., using the REFER method with a Refer-To header). Because URIs come from an unlimited namespace, each service can have its own explicit, finely grained URI. This allows services to be distributed across different providers and discovered dynamically.

For example, an auto-attendant might be sip:attendant@provider.example.com, a specific conference might be sip:conf-123@mixer.example.com, and a voice dialog service might be sip:ivrservice@voiceserver.example.com.
sections.eli5: Instead of secret codes or numbers, everything has a web-like address. You send a request to that address to access a service, like calling a conference room or a voicemail system.
